title: First API call
objectives: keep the key on the server, never the client
tell system and user messages apart
read the text and the stop reason out of a response
handle the errors that will actually happen

steps.instruction: Your app does not hold the model. It sends a message to a computer that does.

pipeline.label: your server
pipeline.note: the only place your key is stored

pipeline.label: the model API
pipeline.note: checks the key, runs the model

pipeline.label: your server
pipeline.note: gets the reply, decides what to show

body: Five stops, and the interesting one is the second.
The browser never talks to the model API. It talks to you.
That middle stop is where the key lives, and where you decide who is allowed to ask.
steps.keypoint: Browser to your server. Your server to the API. Never browser straight to the API.

steps.instruction: This runs in the browser. Tap the line that hands your key to anyone who opens the page.
steps.why: Anything the browser holds, the user can read. The question is fine to show. The key is your account and your money, so it never goes past your server.
steps.after: Bots scan public code for strings starting sk-. This is the most common way beginners lose a key.
steps.keypoint: The question can live in the browser. The key cannot.
skills: keep an API key off the client

steps.instruction: Now the call itself. A request is an object with a few named fields.
body: role is "user" because you are the one talking.
The reply is an object too. The words live at content[0].text.
steps.keypoint: A request names the model, a cap, and the messages. That is the whole thing.

steps.instruction: The whole call, start to finish.
steps.after: That is a working API call. Everything else in this unit is shaping what goes in and checking what comes out.
body: model, max_tokens, messages go in. content[0].text comes out.
Everything else in this unit is shaping what goes in and checking what comes out.

steps.instruction: There is a second place to put words, and it is not a message.
body: system is the standing instruction: who the model is, how it should answer, what shape to use.
messages is the conversation: what was actually said, and by whom.
The user sees the messages. The user never sees the system prompt.
steps.keypoint: system is the job description. messages is the conversation.

steps.instruction: Same question, but now with a system prompt. What changes?
steps.after: Same question, same model, same code. One line of English changed the output.
steps.why: The system prompt asked for one word, so one word came back. The code did not change at all.

steps.instruction: The response carries more than words.
body: stop_reason says why it stopped. end_turn means it finished on its own.
usage says how much text went each way, counted in tokens.
Read both. A reply that stopped for the wrong reason is not an answer.
steps.keypoint: Every reply carries the text, why it stopped, and what it used.

steps.instruction: Now the part every tutorial skips. It will fail, and how it failed matters.

rows: your key is wrong or missing
you sent too many too fast

body: Two of these are your fault and retrying is pointless.
Two are temporary and retrying is exactly right.
Telling them apart is the whole job.
steps.keypoint: 401 and 400 are yours to fix. 429 and 500 are worth retrying.

steps.instruction: Deal each failure into what your code should do.
steps.after: Retrying a 401 fails 401 times, a little more expensively each time.
steps.keypoint: Retry what is temporary. Fix what is yours.

steps.instruction: A 401 means your key is wrong. What does isRetryable say?
steps.after: Four words of logic that stop your app hammering a wall.
steps.why: False, and that is the point. Retrying a bad key fails identically every time, just more expensively.

steps.instruction: And whatever fails, the user must never meet the failure raw.
body: A stack trace tells a student they broke something. They did not.
Return a sentence a person can read, and log the real error where you can find it.
Something is better than nothing: a canned answer beats an empty screen.
steps.keypoint: Degrade, never crash. The user gets a sentence, you get the log.

steps.after: Key on the server, system prompt shaping the answer, stop reason checked. That is a first call done properly.
body: Key on the server, system prompt shaping the answer, stop_reason checked before showing.
